messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Two years ago, Vikram Desai received a phone call that shattered his family’s equilibrium: his younger brother, Arjun, had been killed instantly in a sudden, high-speed collision on the I-95. The violence of the crash and the abruptness of the loss fused into a lingering wound that refused to settle. At first, Vikram told himself he was simply mourning, but grief quickly curdled into a hyper-alert state. Whenever a client mentioned a relative’s recent passing, or a design proposal required him to walk past a local cemetery, his chest would constrict before he could even process the conversation. His body would flare with readiness to flee, heart hammering against his ribs while his mind still tried to place the trigger. These sudden somatic surges, accompanied by brief but vivid flashbacks where the smell of burnt rubber and shattered glass would momentarily overtake the scent of fresh plaster, made him unable to finish the walkthrough. The threat response bypassed his reasoning entirely, leaving him standing in a client’s foyer, dizzy and disoriented. To keep the panic at bay, Vikram began systematically erasing any date tied to October 14th from his calendar and avoiding any conversation that touched on loss. He rescheduled site visits to dodge the anniversary, convincing himself that a scheduling conflict was simply more professional. In his studio, surrounded by swatches and scale models, Vikram could no longer tolerate textures that felt too heavy or colors that leaned toward mourning blacks. He would strip the fabric samples from his mood boards the moment a client brought up a recent bereavement, his hands trembling as he replaced them with neutral tones. The avoidance felt necessary at the time, a way to shield his marriage and his firm’s reputation from his unraveling composure. Yet, the mental space he tried to protect quickly filled with something worse. Lying awake in bed beside his wife, Priya, he would mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios—car crashes, sudden falls, hospital waiting rooms—trying to engineer a sense of control over an uncontrollable world. This relentless worst-case mental scripting only trained his nervous system to anticipate disaster, which in turn made his body react to minor stressors even faster. The cycle deepened across the following months. Every time a grief reminder slipped through his defenses, the resulting threat response pushed him further into preparation and avoidance, which only amplified his baseline alarm. He found himself snapping at Priya over misplaced keys, his irritability flaring into sharp, uncharacteristic outbursts that left him feeling guilty. Professionally, the strain became impossible to hide. When a long-time client, a widow grieving her husband, requested memorial pendants of dark marble for her new living room, Vikram’s throat closed up and his vision blurred with that familiar, intrusive flash of Arjun’s last moments. Fearing a collapse on the job site, he began declining any design project that required emotional labor, retreating to sterile, colorless spaces he could navigate without fear of breaking down. The constant rehearsal and avoidance had become a self-reinforcing trap, tightening his grip on his own life even as it frayed. By the second anniversary, the carefully constructed barriers had become a cage. Vikram’s relentless mental preparation and his avoidance of any conversation touching on loss had drained his marriage of intimacy and threatened his firm’s standing. He realized he could no longer outmaneuver the dread, nor could he explain why his hands shook every time a news report mentioned a highway accident. Seeking help felt like admitting the walls he had built were failing. He walked into the clinic hoping to dismantle the loop before it cost him his career or his marriage, desperate to find a way to remember his brother without feeling like he was dying all over again.
